title: CRLA/354/2014 of Vijay Singh Rawat Vs State Of Uttarakhand

paras.text:
Reserved on:03.07.2019
 Delivered on:25.07.2019
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Appeal No. 354 of 2014
Vijay Singh Rawat .......Appellant
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand .......Respondent
Mr. R.S. Sammal, Advocate assisted by Ms. Sarita Bisht, Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. V.K. Gemini, Deputy Advocate General with Mr. Pankaj Joshi Brief Holder for the State of
Uttarakhand.
Coram:Hon'ble Alok Singh, J.
 Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
Per: Ravindra Maithani, J. (Oral)
This appeal is preferred against the judgment and order
dated 01.10.2014/10.10.2014, passed by the court of learned Sessions
Judge, Bageshwar, in Sessions Trial No. 219 of 2014, State Vs. Vijay
Singh Rawat. By the impugned judgment and order, the appellant has
been convicted under Section 376 2(k)(l) and 506 IPC and sentenced
as hereunder:-
(i) Under Section 376 2(l) IPC rigorous
imprisonment for life, which shall mean,
imprisonment for the remainder of the
appellant's natural life and with a fine of
Rs.10,000/-. In default of payment of fine,
to undergo imprisonment for a further
period of six months.
(ii) Under Section 506 (2) IPC, with rigorous
imprisonment for four years and a fine of
Rs.5,000/-. In default of payment of fine, to
undergo imprisonment for a further period
of two months.

2
2. Prosecution case, briefly stated is that on 01.04.2014, an
FIR under Sections 376 and 506 IPC was lodged at reporting out
post, Kannadi Devi, Police Station Bageshwar by PW 1. According
to it, four months prior to that day, the appellant forcibly raped the
sister of the first informant and threatened her that if she discloses it
to anyone, he would kill her. On 23.03.2014, the victim was
medically examined and then it was revealed that she was pregnant
for about 4-5 months. Based on it, Case Crime No. 12 of 2014, under
Sections 376 and 506 IPC was registered. The victim was examined
under Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
(hereinafter referred to as "the Code"). She was also medically
examined on 02.04.2014. The Investigating Officer prepared the site
plan, arrested the appellant and submitted charge-sheet against him.
In the sessions trial, on 13.05.2014, once charges were framed, which
were subsequently amended on 24.07.2014. Appellant was charged
for the offences under Sections 376 (2)(k)(l) and 506 IPC, to which,
he denied and claimed trial.
3. In order to prove the case, prosecution examined, as
many as, five witnesses namely, PW 1 brother of the victim, PW 2
the victim, PW 3 Dr. Gayatri Pangati, PW 4 Harish Prasad, PW 5 S.I.
Pratibha Bhatt.
4. Appellant was examined under Section 313 of the Code.
According to the appellant, he has been falsely implicated. Appellant
has not adduced any evidence in his defence. After hearing the

3
parties vide impugned judgment and order, the appellant has been
convicted and sentenced, as hereinbefore. Aggrieved, the instant
appeal.
5. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
records.
6. Learned counsel for the appellant would argue that the
appellant has been falsely implicated in the case; the victim did not
tell it to the Investigating Officer that the act of sexual intercourse
was without her consent; statement under Section 164 of the Code is
false and cannot be believed; the victim did not reveal the incident
for four months, till her pregnancy was detected, which makes her
statement wholly unreliable; the victim had no reason for not
disclosing it to anyone in the village or to resist the act, further. The
statements of the victim are not corroborated from any other
evidence; it is not a case in which conviction may be based solely on
the statement of the victim. Therefore, it is argued that the
prosecution utterly failed to prove the case against the appellant and
the court below committed an error in convicting and sentencing the
appellant therefore, the appeal deserves to be allowed.
7. On the other hand, learned State counsel would argue
that the victim is a handicapped, who was staying all alone in the
village; the appellant took advantage of her disability, raped and
threatened her; the victim was quite innocent, she never knew, the
meaning of the act, as such; since appellant had threatened her to life,

4
the victim could not muster the courage to disclose the act to anyone,
until her pregnancy was detected; the statement of the victim is
believable and the prosecution has been able to prove the charges
against the appellant. Learned court below has not committed any
error in convicting and sentencing the appellant, therefore, the appeal
deserves to be dismissed.
8. PW 1 is the brother of the victim. According to him, his
sister is handicapped, who was staying all alone at the relevant time.
She had no neighbours and his sister revealed it to him that seven
months ago, the appellant entered into her house and forcibly,
sexually assaulted her, due to which, she became pregnant.
Thereafter, this witness lodged the FIR. PW 2 is the victim herself,
she states that 7-8 months prior to the date when her statement was
recorded, when all were asleep in the night, the appellant opened the
door and entered in her house; disrobed her and gagged her mouth
and thereafter, inserted his penis into her vagina. According to PW 2,
the victim, the appellant also threatened her, that if she reveals it to
anyone, he would kill her. She became pregnant; she also states that
the appellant raped her without her consent or permission. She
proved her statement recorded under Section 164 of the Code.
9. The Court also made observations with regard to the
condition of the victim. According to it, her face was disfigured;
shape of the nose and upper lip was absent; she was able to
understands the questions and reply them. Her voice was not clear,

5
but understandable. Upon having been asked by the court, she
revealed that in her childhood, while bursting the fire crackers, her
face was disfigured. Her parents had died, she was an orphan and
could not get her medical treatment done, therefore, her face is
disfigured.
10. PW 3 Dr. Gayatri Pangati examined the victim on
01.04.2014 at district hospital Bageshwar. She found that the victim
was seven months pregnant. PW 4 is Harish Prasad is a formal
witness, who proved chick FIR and entry in the general diary.
11. PW 5 SI Pratibha Bhatt is the Investigating Officer,
according to her; she investigated the case; prepared the site plan;
arrested the appellant; got her medically examined and her statement
were recorded under Section 164 of the Code. PW 5 SI Pratibha
Bhatt, proved the charge-sheet.
12. The learned court below took into consideration the
provision of Section 114-A of The Indian Evidence Act, 1872
(hereinafter referred to as "the Act") with regard to presumption of
no consent.
13. A few things are to be kept in mind while appreciating
evidence in the instant case. This is an incident of a village in the
Uttarakhand hills. The victim is a woman of about 30 years, who had
lost her parents. The victim's face is disfigured, due to bursting of
fire crackers in her childhood. She can hear or understand. She did

6
depose before the Court and Court had made these observations.
Though her voice is not clear, at the relevant time, she was staying
all alone. There is evidence to the effect that though there are houses
around the house of the victim but those houses are not occupied by
anyone, they are old houses, except one house, which was under
construction.
14. Appellant is not some stranger to the victim. PW 1,
brother of the victim in his cross-examination states that grandfather
of this witness and the appellant was one and the same. They are, in
fact, cousins and, so are the appellant and the victim.
15. During the trial itself, on 17.07.2014, the victim
delivered a baby boy. At the time of argument, learned counsel for
the appellant would inform the Court that victim as well as her child
had already died due to some reasons.
16. FIR is delayed. The question of consent is also for
consideration and also the applicability of Section 114-A of the Act.
17. In case of State of Himachal Pradesh Vs. Shree Kant
Shekari (2004) 8 SCC 153, the Court, inter-alia, held as hereunder:-
"18............Delay in lodging the first information report
cannot be used as a ritualistic formula for discarding the
prosecution case and doubting its authenticity. It only puts the
court on guard to search for and consider if any explanation has
been offered for the delay. Once it is offered, the court is to only
see whether it is satisfactory or not. In case if the prosecution fails
to satisfactorily explain the delay and there is possibility of
embellishment for exaggeration in the prosecution version on

7
account of such delay, it is a relevant factor. On the other hand,
satisfactory explanation of the delay is weighty enough to reject
the plea of false implication or vulnerability of the prosecution
case. As the factual scenario shows, the victim was totally
unaware of the catastrophe which had befallen her. That being so,
the mere delay in lodging of the first information report does not
in any way render the prosecution version brittle. These aspects
were highlighted in Tulshidas Kanolkar v. State of Goa4
."
18. In the case of Raju and others Vs. State of Madhya
Pradesh, (2008) 15 SCC 133 making reference to Section 114-A of
the Act, the Hon'ble Court, inter-alia, held that the statement of
victim cannot be taken as a gospel truth. The Court observed as
hereunder:-
"12.......... It is however significant that Section 113-A
and 113-B too were inserted in the Evidence Act by the same
amendment by which certain presumptions in the cases of
abetment of suicide and dowry death have been raised against the
accused. These two sections, thus, raise a clear presumption in
favour of the prosecution but no similar presumption with respect
to rape is visualized as the presumption under Section 114-A is
extremely restricted in its applicability. This clearly shows that
insofar as allegations of rape are concerned, the evidence of a
prosecutrix, must be examined as that of an injured witness
whose presence at the spot is probable but it can never be
presumed that her statement should, without exception, be taken
as the gospel truth. Additionally, her statement can, at best, be
adjudged on the principle that ordinarily no injured witness would
tell a lie or implicate a person falsely. We believe that it is under
these principles that this case, and others such as this one, need to
be examined...................."
19. In the case of Munna Vs. State of Madhya Pradesh
(2014) 10 SCC 254, also Hon'ble Court observed with regard to
presumption under Section 114-A of the Act, vis-à-vis, the statement
of the victim, which is as hereunder:-
"11.Thus, while absence of injuries or absence of raising
alarm or delay in FIR may not by itself be enough to disbelieve
the version of prosecutrix in view of the statutory presumption
under Section 114-A of the Evidence Act but if such statement
has inherent infirmities, creating doubt about its veracity, the
same may not be acted upon.........................."
4. (2003) 8 SCC 590: 2004 SCC (Cri.) 44

8
20. It would be pertinent to note at this stage that
prosecution according to the victim was handicapped and PW 5 has
also proved a certificate to that effect, which is Ex-A 11, given by
district Social Welfare Officer. According to which the victim was
more than 40% handicapped and she was being paid handicapped
pension. Categorically, it has not been stated or proved on behalf of
the prosecution as to what was the reason for terming her as a
handicapped person. It has not been shown or proved that she is
orthopedic or visually handicapped. What the Court observed and
what is stated is that her face was disfigured, she had no upper lip or
shape of nose but she could hear and understand and speak as well,
though her voice was unclear. It appears that because of this reason
she is being termed as handicapped person. This is important because
the charge against the appellant is under Section 376 2 (k) (l). These
sub-sections are as hereunder:-
 "376 (2) Whoever,-
 .....................................................................
 .....................................................................
 (k) being in a position of control or dominance over a
 woman, commits rape on such woman; or
 (l) commits rape on a woman suffering from mental or
 physical disability; or
.....................................................................
..................................................................."

21. The above provision reveals that on the one hand sub-section (k) makes provision when offence is committed by a person
who is in possession or control of dominance over the victim.
Whereas sub-section (l) makes provision, if the victim is suffering
from mental or physical disability.

9
22. It is being stated by the victim and her brother that she
was forcibly raped. The victim has stated that she had not consented
or permitted for the act of sexual intercourse.
23. In the case of Deelip Singh @ Dilip Kumar Vs. State of
Bihar (2005), 1 SCC 88, Hon'ble Court has observed as to what does
consent mean. It was held as hereunder:-
"22. In Words and Phrases, Permanent Edn., Vol. 8-A, the
following passages culled out from certain old decisions of the
American courts are found:
"...adult female's understanding of nature and
consequences of sexual act must be intelligent understanding to
constitute 'consent'.
Consent within penal law, defining rape, requires exercise
of intelligence based on knowledge of its significance and moral
quality and there must be a choice between resistance and
assent..."
23. It was observed by B.P. Singh, J. speaking for the
Court in Uday v. State of Karnatka1
: (SCC p. 53, para 12)
12. The courts in India have by and large adopted
these tests to discover whether the consent was voluntary
or whether it was vitiated so as not to be legal consent."
24. There is a good analysis of the expression "consent"
in the context of Section 375 IPC by Tekchand, J. in Rao
Harnarain Singh Sheoji Singh v. State2
. The learned Judge had
evidently drawn inspiration from the above passages in the law
dictionaries. The observation of the learned Judge (AIR p. 126,
para 7) that
"there is a difference between consent and
submission [and] every consent involves a submission but
the converse does not follow and a mere act of submission
does not involve consent",
is quite apposite. The said proposition is virtually a
repetition of what was said by Coleridge, J. in R. v. Day3
in 1841 as quoted in Words and Phrases (Permanent Edn.)
at p. 205. The following remarks in Harnarain case2 are
also pertinent: (AIR p. 126, para 7)
Consent is an act of reason accompanied by
deliberation, a mere act of helpless resignation in the face
of inevitable compulsion, non-resistance and passive
giving in cannot be deemed to be consent."
On the facts, it was held that there was resistance by
the prosecutrix and there was no voluntary participation in
the sexual act. That case would therefore fall more
appropriately within clause first of Section 375."
1 (2003) 4 SCC 46 : 2003 SCC (Cri) 775 : (2003) 2 Scale 329
2 AIR 1958 Punj 123 : 1958 Cri LJ 563 : 59 Punj LR 519
3 (1841) 9 C&P 722 : 173 ER 1026

10
24. To be a consent within penal law, it requires exercise of
intelligence based on knowledge of its significance and moral quality
and there must be a choice between resistance and consent. Consent
and submission are two terms quite apart, so is submission. Consent
may be there only when one makes a choice between to do or not to
do. It is an act, which is exercised independently, to any external
pressure or factor; it should be an independent choice, a decision."
25. In the case of Deepak Gulati Vs. State of Haryana,
(2013) 7 SCC 675, the Hon'ble Court, inter-alia, held that the
consent may be expressed or implied, coursed or mis-guided.
"21. Consent may be express or implied, coerced or
misguided, obtained willingly or through deceit. Consent is an act
of reason, accompanied by deliberation, the mind weighing, as in
a balance, the good and evil on each side...................."
26. The biggest choice, this Court has to make is as to
whether the delay has been explained, satisfactorily? Whether it was
an act under consent. During the course of the arguments, learned
counsel for the appellant has argued that since, the victim was
staying all alone was not married, it was her biological need also and
this is where she made a choice to have sex with the appellant. It is
an act of consensual sex, its not rape. It is argued that since, parties
were living in a village, appellant was a cousin of the victim, it
cannot be presumed that the victim was, in fact, constantly under
some fear, for not disclosing this act for so long. It is also argued that
her statement cannot be believed.

11
27. In FIR, it is stated that some 4-5 months prior to that
date, the appellant raped the victim. PW 2, the victim was examined
under Section 164 of the Code, on 03.04.2014. What she stated was
that about seven months prior to her examination, the appellant did
Galat Kaam, "Zabardasti" with her and thereafter the appellant used
to visit quite often her house and do the Galat Kaam and threaten her
that in case, she reveals it to anyone he would kill her. She has stated
that she is bearing appellants' child. In her re-examination in the
court, PW 2, the victim has stated in the month of July, 2014 she
delivered a baby boy. The statement of the victim need to be
scrutinized a little more carefully before it is accepted. In the FIR, it
is stated that once the appellant raped the victim, whereas in her
statement under Section 164 of the Code, the victim has stated that
repeatedly she was raped by the appellant, when she said that after
the first incident of rape the appellant used to visit her house and do
the Galat Kam. When asked in the court, in her re-examination on
06.08.2014, the victim has stated that the appellant raped her twice
though she was not clear. Firstly, she said that the appellant raped her
only once but then she says that she was raped twice. The appellant
had threatened her that he would kill her and her brother, in case she
reveals it to anyone. PW 5 S.I. Pratibha Bhatt, is the Investigating
Officer, in her cross-examination she states that on being questioned
the victim had told it to her that she was raped only once. This
variation in the statement of the victim, this self-contradiction gains
more importance. In FIR its, one act of rape, in her statement under

12
Section 164 of the Code, its repeated act and in Court though she was
not clear but finally she says that she was raped twice. This statement
may be termed as wavering. Whereas, PW 5, the Investigating
Officer says that the victim had told it to her that she was raped only
once. This self-contradiction is not on some insignificant or
immaterial point, its very significant contradiction.
28. Learned counsel for the appellant has also urged that,
the victim never did tell it to the Investigating Officer that she was
forcibly raped. In fact, when questioned victim told that she had told
it to the Investigating Officer that the rape was without her consent
but the Investigating Officer says that victim never told it to her that
without her consent or permission, she was raped. According to the
Investigating Officer, the victim did not tell it to her that after
disrobing and gagging her mouth, the appellant inserted his penis
into the vagina of the victim. Why the victim did not reveal to
anyone in the village or to her brother that she was forcibly raped
once or twice. As stated the number of acts are not established, the
statement of the victim is wavering, inconsistent or self-contradictory
on this aspect. According to PW 5, the Investigating Officer, the
victim had told it to her that she would abort the fetous and had not
told it to her the act was without her consent or permission. Who was
threatened? In FIR and in her statement initially the victim says that
the appellant had threatened to her life but when examined further on
06.08.2014, she states that the appellant had threatened to kill her
and her brother. Variation or contradiction seems to be small but it

13
has great significance because, according to the prosecution due to
this fear only, the victim could not reveal the act to anyone earlier.
What was the threat, it is in doubt. Victim and appellants were
cousins. The background is important. It's a village of hills. Why
was the victim so afraid of the appellant? Why she did not reveal it to
anyone, what prevented her?
29. According to PW 2, the victim her statement was
recorded before the Magistrate under Section 164 of the Code. She
proved it and in her cross-examination when asked she said, when
her statement was recorded her brother namely, PW 1 was not
present. Whereas, PW 1 the brother of the victim states that when the
statement of the victim was being recorded before the Magistrate, she
was along with his sister and the Magistrate had also enquired from
him. The Magistrate had said that since, she was not able to
understand the language of the victim, the statement was recorded as
to what was stated by this witness, PW 1. PW 2, the victim says that
her brother was not present with her when her statement was
recorded before the Magistrate. But on the other hand, PW 1 the
brother of the victim says that it is he, who got the statement
recorded because the Magistrate was not able to understand the
language of the victim; why is this contradiction. These
contradictions in the statement makes this Court to believe that, in
fact, statement of PW 2, the victim is not wholly reliable. It in itself
cannot be made basis of conviction. DNA of the foetus was not got
done, although the appellant denied that he would be ready to get his

14
DNA examination done but, its also does not make any difference for
the simple reason that what is being argued is that it was consensual
act. Court cannot presume that the victim is not in a position to take
any decision, she has been independently living. The explanation of
delay in the case is not satisfactory, the threat perception which is
being put, does not seem to be as such, which could have an impact
of preventing the victim from disclosing or revealing the act to
anyone in the village or at least to his brother PW 1.
30. In the case of Vijayan Vs. State of Kerala (2008) 14
SCC 763. The question was with regard to rape under the promise of
marriage. An FIR was lodged after seven months. The Hon'ble
Court, inter-alia, has held as hereunder:-
"The present case wholly depends upon the testimony of
the prosecutrix. The incident in the present case took place seven
months prior to the date of lodging the complaint as a realization
dawned upon her that she has been subjected to rape by the
appellant-accused. No complaint or grievance was made either to
the police or the parents prior thereto. The explanation for delay
in lodging the FIR is that the appellant-accused promised her to
marry therefore the FIR was not filed. In cases where the sole
testimony of the prosecutrix is available, it is very dangerous to
convict the accused, specially when the prosecutrix could venture
to wait for seven months for filing the FIR for rape. This leaves
the accused totally defenceless. Had the prosecutrix lodged the
complaint soon after the incident, there would have been some
supporting evidence like the medical report or any other injury on
the body of the prosecutrix so as to show the sign of rape. If the
prosecutrix has willingly submitted herself to sexual intercourse
and waited for seven months for filing the FIR it will be very
hazardous to convict on such sole oral testimony..............."
31. In the instant case, the delay has not been found to be
satisfactorily explained. The statement of PW 2, the victim is not
wholly reliable, it has self-contradictions variations, her statement is
wavering. The victim did not tell it to the Investigating Officer that

15
the act was without her consent. What she said to the Investigating
Officer was that she would get the foetus aborted. In view of the
above discussion, this Court is of the view that solely on the basis of
the statement of PW 1, the victim the appellant cannot be convicted.
The prosecution has failed to prove the charges leveled against the
appellant and the appellant ought to have been acquitted of all the
charges. The learned court below committed an error in convicting
and sentencing the appellant, therefore, the appeal deserves to be
allowed.
32. The appeal is allowed and Judgment and order dated
01.10.2014/10.10.2014 passed by the court of learned Sessions
Judge, Bageshwar in Sessions Trial No. 219 of 2014, State Vs. Sh.
Vijay Singh Rawat is hereby set aside. The appellant is acquitted of
all the charges.
33. Appellant is in jail. If he is not wanted in any other case,
he would be released forthwith.
34. Let a copy of the judgment be sent to the court below
for compliance.
(Ravindra Maithani, J.) (Alok Singh, J.) Shubham
